hansvm 7 hours ago | parent | next [–]

Pure speculation on a few possible explanations (noting that TFA describes ordinary exercise as generating enough squishing force, any other actions the researchers did being to isolate the causal factor):

1. Mammals don't naturally exist in environments where exercise isn't mandatory. _Some_ system had to generate those compounds, and there was never any pressure to keep it from being tied to the other stress-related changes bones undergo (like density changes). Once it evolved once somewhere in some critter once via that machinery, the advantage was large enough that it was locked in.

2. Exercise directly contributes inflammatory factors. Tying the cure to those to a measure of exercise intensity (bone squishing) helps calibrate the dosage. Even if an imperfect measure, the proxy of bone loading might confer some advantage in, e.g., not wasting energy on unnecessary proteins.

3. Exercise indirectly suggests a resource-poor environment, leading to lower chance of offspring succeeding and needing longer lives to produce enough viable offspring. The compounds in question aren't free to produce, so there's an advantage in only providing them to organisms who will meaningfully benefit. Mind you, resource-poor environments often promote shorter lifespans and faster growth cycles as an evolutionary trait, _but_ without a mechanism to force your offspring to mature more quickly the osteocyte-mediated lifespan could allow for resource-dependent lifetime offspring counts.

4. The mechanism could have evolved for unrelated reasons, perhaps directly contributing to the bone density calibration osteocytes already mediate. Any impact on lifespan is incidental or otherwise produces less evolutionary pressure for or against the feature than the direct purpose of the compounds.

5. More than having evolved for unrelated reasons, the fact that the compounds have any effect at all might not be evolutionarily selected for. We produce plenty of unimportant metabolic byproducts that we don't particularly care about, and it could be that some more important osteocyte function incidentally produces these "waste" proteins.

radford-neal 1 hour ago | root | parent | next [–]

Evolution is the unifying concept underlying all of biology. Finding and testing evolutionary explanations may be difficult, but not looking for such explanations is akin to saying to someone speculating about why, say, some wooden structures are stronger than others, that "I find these explanations of physical effects in terms of gravity and electromagnetism very unconvincing". Wood is a complex material, so understanding its properties is difficult. But if your explanation of wood's properties is incompatible with fundamental physics then there's something wrong with it.

Similarly, explanations of aging that amount to "the body just for no reason fails to do something that it easily could even though it's obviously beneficial" are pretty much like explanations of physical processes that violate conservation of mass/energy. There had better be some possible evolutionary explanation, since otherwise it's very likely that the result is due to some experimental error.

hansvm 49 minutes ago | root | parent | prev | next [–]

> unfalsifiable

If we're trying to piece together how the past actually happened based on the shadow it left on the present, yes, falsifiability is hard, sometimes possible to achieve. Most of the speculations I provided could be reasonably well tested though.

Take (5) as an example. If you find other important byproducts from the associated genes, those strengthen (5)'s argument. If you find significant negative effects from the new "miracle" proteins, those strengthen (5)'s argument. If you find an organism with an energetically intensive mechanism for removing these new "miracle" proteins, those strengthen (5)'s argument. If you apply a medicinal intervention to allow the gene to be enabled but those particular "miracle" proteins to be disabled in a wild population and observe the gene frequency dwindle, that strengthens (5)'s argument.

None of it's perfect, but there are a variety of experiments and observations you can do to strengthen or weaken your belief in specific causal mechanisms.

> used to justify unjustifiable positions

I go back and forth on this one. Should you hide information (in this case, not even very good information, just plausible mechanisms, provided because somebody was a bit curious and I thought scratching that itch might help them on whatever journey they're currently undertaking) just because it's possible to misunderstand it? Because it's prone to misuse?

Like, obviously if people are concluding from a list of guesses appropriately described as such that osteocytes evolved to extend life as a poorly calibrated part of the exercise process, that's not justified. What happens when people extend similar wild speculation to gender or racial differences? You're right, it's a touchy subject.

On the other hand, that's an argument against:

- Data-driven organizations -- a common cognitive bias is the spotlight effect, and applied to "data-driven" organizations it often leads to abandoning intuition and reason when the best proxy measurements you're able to perform incorrectly suggest a different course of action to be optimal.

- Giving correct estimates to your PM -- you know the organization will run more smoothly if you start unraveling the spaghetti sitting in fromt of you, but (in many orgs) it'll take longer to argue that point than it will to just do your job correctly, so you fudge ticket descriptions and estimates to make sure critical maintenance happens.

I try to evaluate that sort of thing on a case-by-case basis. I think it's fine here. I don't have a good justification for why I think that.

personalityson 4 hours ago | parent | prev | next [–]

The skeleton is economical:

Repair pays off only when the skeleton is used -- we can invest in repair because we know the animal is active/foraging and we will get paid back on the investment.

Low loading is a sign that we should cut back on maintenance -- the animal is sick, injured, starving etc and it's better to conserve energy.

The optimal amount of exercise is what tells your body to invest in repair, without acquiring repair debt. Sedentary life is the misleading signal, because it tells the body you're declining when you aren't.

waterheater 8 hours ago | parent | next [–]

It's not quite vice grips; I had to dig into the paper to understand it. Their specific DTAL protocol provided "moderate mechanical loading" of "2 N at 2 Hz for 300 cycles, twice/week, [for] 3 months". For reference, a 200g stationary object exerts that much force on a surface due to gravity. With 300 cycles at 2Hz, the exercises lasted for 150 seconds, or 2.5 minutes, and the exercises occurred twice a week.

Note, however, that their experimental model section says they applied axial force (think columns, not joists) to the tibia using an ElectroForce 3300 (https://www.tainstruments.com/3330-system/) while the mice were under anesthesia. From this, it seems like they knocked out the mice and placed their legs underneath a mechanical ram to apply axial compressive forces.

Because people are typically awake when exercising, given that muscles are designed to carry forces around the skeleton, I imagine, even after scaling from a mice to a human purely by sizing, the human force equivalent will be many times higher.

If you're looking to try this out for yourself, the seated leg press will most closely simulate the study's method. Figure out what "moderate" loading is for you, and shoot for 3 sets x 10 reps at least twice a week. Overall, choose skeletally-compressive exercises where you're "pushing," such as weighted squats (e.g. barbell squats) and any type of "press" exercise like the leg press, chest press, military press, and even cycling (you push your pedals). For the purposes of this study, avoid exercises with any pulling motion, including pull-ups, pull-downs, rows, and swimming.

From a force perspective, running has some compressive elements, but the load comes from gravity alone, and good runners minimize compressive forces. Since running therefore is primarily a pulling exercise, I can sort of see what they're getting at.

Windchaser 1 hour ago | root | parent [–]

"..and eaten"

Probably not effective, our gut is very good at splicing up proteins into constituent amino acids.

If you want specific proteins/peptides in your bloodstream*, for now the most reliable way is generally to inject them.

But yeah, it is very much not necessarily the case that our own bodies will produce the same proteins under similar exercise, or that the mouse proteins released would have the same effects in us as in them, or that proteins released under similar exercise would actually de-age us.

It's interesting to track down the mechanisms in mice (exercise induces protein release - how? - which then de-ages the mice - also, how?) but you have to reproduce the work entirely separately in humans. Not just because it might not work, but because it is very important (and neat!) to understand the biochemical mechanisms of human ageing and de-ageing, and that understanding of How Things Work is a big part of the long-term reward.

[*] I'm not advocating for injecting untested/unregulated proteins or peptides, only speaking of ROA, route of administration
